Fake ASOS Website Scam UK: Spot a Copycat Store

Criminals are running fake ASOS websites that look almost identical to the real thing—but one wrong click could cost you hundreds of pounds and put your identity at risk.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-05-10 · Updated 2026-08-06 · 10 min read

Quick answer: ASOS's UK help page says ASOS Sample Sale at asossamplesale.com is part of ASOS, so ASOS plus sale words is not enough to decide. Start from ASOS's UK Customer Care page to confirm a site, and check asos.com orders in My Orders. Screenshot suspicious pages and contact your card issuer promptly.
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Use the right recovery route. Follow the payment, account and identity checklist; reporting differs in Scotland.

ASOS plus a sale word decides nothing

ASOS says ordinary ASOS shopping takes place at asos.com, but its UK help page also identifies asossamplesale.com as the official ASOS Sample Sale. A name containing ASOS, outlet, sale or clearance is therefore neither proof of legitimacy nor proof of fraud. Start from ASOS's UK Customer Care page and follow the official link it publishes.

The Sample Sale help pages put it plainly: ASOS Sample Sale is part of ASOS.com, and the Sample Sale terms say the contract is with ASOS.com Limited and that all products offered there are ASOS products. That is why a word test cannot work in either direction — reading the letters in an address will not separate an ASOS-run sale from somebody else's shop wearing ASOS branding. What replaces it is a habit: reach an address the way ASOS publishes it, not the way an advert offers it.

The verification route, step by step

  • Open a fresh tab and type asos.com by hand. Do not arrive from a search advert, a social post, an email or a message.
  • Go to Customer Care from there, and look for the official links ASOS itself publishes for shopping and for its Sample Sale.
  • Compare the address you were sent against the one ASOS publishes, character for character. A near miss is a miss.
  • If it appears nowhere in ASOS's own help pages, treat it as unverified and keep your card details to yourself.
  • Still unsure? Ask ASOS Customer Care through the official site before paying, not after.

This works because it takes your judgement out of the loop. Copied logos, lifted product photography and a working basket are cheap to assemble, so how convincing a page looks carries almost no information — where you got the address from carries all of it. NCSC guidance on shopping and paying safely online makes the same point about deceptive shopping sites: navigate to a retailer independently instead of trusting a link you were handed.

Reading a web address, and what that can and cannot settle

Reading an address is worth learning, as long as you know what it proves. The owner is the part immediately to the left of the first single slash. In asos.shop-deals.example/sale the owner is shop-deals.example, and every character further left — brand names included — is decoration chosen by whoever holds it.

These are warning signs to resolve against ASOS's own help pages, never verdicts on their own:

  • The brand pushed into a subdomain, so it reads as ASOS at a glance.
  • The right name with a different ending welded on, such as .shop, .online or .com.co.
  • A country or year tag that makes the address look like a regional ASOS site.
  • A brand plus sale word combination — the one that genuinely cannot be read, because ASOS publishes its own Sample Sale address.
  • A padlock in the address bar, which certifies encryption and nothing about honesty. Certificates are free.

Checking an `asos.com` order, and the limit of that check

An order placed through asos.com should appear in the correct ASOS account under My Orders. ASOS Sample Sale orders use a separate account and do not appear there. If an expected asos.com order is missing, check that you used the right account and contact ASOS Customer Care through the official site before deciding what happened.

ASOS documents where an ordinary order lives: My Account, then My Orders, then Track parcel, with the estimated delivery date shown in the account and in the confirmation email. ASOS Sample Sale is explicit that its orders sit outside that view — you will not see Sample Sale orders on an ASOS.com account, and viewing them means creating a separate Sample Sale account. A blank My Orders page is therefore a prompt to check which account and which ASOS service you used, not evidence that nothing was bought from ASOS.

Treat the messages around an order the same way. ASOS's help pages warn that people impersonate it through social media, free webmail accounts, WhatsApp and fake sites, and say ASOS contacts customers through an ASOS-branded email address or a verified social account. A confirmation email proves little on its own, because whoever built a fake shop also wrote its emails.

If you entered personal details on a site you now doubt

A fashion checkout collects more than a card number: a name, a delivery address, a contact number, often a password for a new account. Rather than guessing what will be done with any of it, treat what you typed as exposed and close the openings you control.

  • Change the password anywhere you reused whatever you set on that site, starting with the email account attached to it.
  • If card details went in, ring your card issuer on the number printed on the card or shown in its own app, and ask about stopping the card and watching the account.
  • Keep the confirmation page and everything that arrives afterwards, and check any claim about the order by returning to the address you typed yourself.

Cifas Protective Registration, which costs £30 for two years, is a narrower step, not a routine response to every suspicious checkout. It is a paid service running for two years that places a warning flag against your name and details so participating organisations carry out extra checks, and Cifas presents it as a measure for people at heightened risk of identity fraud. It is not insurance, and it does not guarantee every application in your name will be checked.

Legal rights may be hard to enforce against an untraceable seller

Statutory rights do not vanish because a trader used a brand's name without permission. GOV.UK sets out the usual distance-sale sequence for an online purchase: tell the trader you are cancelling within 14 days of receiving the goods, send them back within a further 14 days, and receive the refund within 14 days of the trader receiving the goods or evidence that you returned them. The standard delivery charge you paid is refundable, and exceptions and possible deductions still apply.

The difficulty is the trader, not the right. A cancellation notice needs somebody to serve it on, and a seller hiding behind a lookalike address may not reply, may publish no returns address, and may not be identifiable at all. Where a reply does arrive and makes the refund conditional on confirming your card number, or on installing software so the money can be sent, that is a continuation of the same approach rather than a resolution — and your realistic route then runs through the payment instead of the seller.

If you already paid

Screenshot the shop while it is still standing — the product page, the basket total, the address bar — and keep the advert or message that delivered you there. Sites like this are built to disappear.

Then look at how the money left. Section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act 1974 may apply, never automatically, to a purchase funded by credit. It needs the required relationship between the credit and the supplier, plus a cash price — counted per item, or per qualifying set — of more than £100 and no more than £30,000. MoneyHelper explains that an intermediary in the payment chain can affect whether cover exists at all, and the Financial Ombudsman Service has reported that misunderstanding credit protection has cost consumers money.

So a £45 clothing order sits under the price test whatever card paid for it, and a credit card alone does not make a claim valid.

Chargeback is a card-scheme process rather than a statutory entitlement, with rules and deadlines set by the scheme, so raise it with your issuer promptly instead of waiting to see whether a parcel turns up. Money sent by bank transfer for clothing is the hardest version of this: tell your bank the same day.

If poor-quality goods did arrive, keep them — they are evidence, and what a counterfeit means for a refund is covered separately. The scam recovery checklist puts the payment, account and identity steps in order.

Where to report a copycat ASOS shop

Tell ASOS through the Customer Care pages you reach by typing asos.com, so the brand knows the address is circulating. Then use the public routes:

  • A suspicious website goes to the NCSC, through its reporting form for scam websites.
  • A paid advert goes to the Advertising Standards Authority. Flagging it inside the platform that served it is a useful extra step rather than a substitute.
  • A phishing email goes to report@phishing.gov.uk.
  • A suspicious SMS text can be forwarded to 7726 free of charge, and your mobile network will look into the sender.
  • Lost money belongs in a fraud report. Report Fraud takes them online at reportfraud.police.uk and on 0300 123 2040; readers in Scotland should call Police Scotland on 101 instead.

Frequently asked questions

Is asossamplesale.com a real ASOS website?

Yes. ASOS's Sample Sale help pages say ASOS Sample Sale is part of ASOS.com, and its terms say the contract is with ASOS.com Limited and that all products offered there are ASOS products. That is exactly why the word test fails: an address pairing the ASOS name with a sale word can be genuine. Confirm any address from ASOS's UK Customer Care page rather than from the words in it.

An advert sent me to an "ASOS outlet" address. Is it a copycat?

Not automatically, and not automatically genuine either. Because ASOS publishes its own Sample Sale address, the words prove nothing in either direction. Open a fresh tab, type asos.com, go to Customer Care and see whether the address you were sent matches a link ASOS itself publishes. If it does not appear there, do not pay.

I received an order confirmation email. Doesn't that make the shop real?

Not on its own, because whoever built a fake shop also wrote its emails. ASOS says it contacts customers through an ASOS-branded email address or a verified social media account, so free webmail or a WhatsApp number announcing itself as ASOS customer care does not match that description. Check the order in the account it was placed with, and ask ASOS Customer Care through the official site.

My order is not in My Orders. Does that prove no order was placed with ASOS?

No. An order placed through asos.com should appear in the correct ASOS account under My Orders, but ASOS Sample Sale orders use a separate Sample Sale account and do not appear there. Check that you signed in to the right account, then contact ASOS Customer Care through the official site before deciding what happened.

Is asos.shop-deals.example an ASOS address?

No. The owner of a web address is the part immediately to the left of the first single slash, which here is shop-deals.example. Everything further left, brand names included, is decoration the site chose for itself. Reading the address this way rules an address out; confirming one in ASOS's own help pages is what rules it in.

I paid £45 by debit card and nothing arrived. Where does that leave me?

Below the Section 75 cash-price test, which needs more than £100, and on a debit card rather than a credit agreement. Ask your bank about chargeback instead, since card schemes set their own rules and deadlines for it, and raise it promptly. Report the loss as well so the site is on record.

Is it worth reporting a copycat if I never bought anything?

Yes, and it costs nothing. Send the address to the NCSC through its reporting form for scam websites, tell ASOS through its Customer Care pages, and take a paid advert to the Advertising Standards Authority as well as reporting it inside the platform that ran it.
